# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The rapid expansion of transcatheter therapies for structural heart disease has been accompanied by an increasing need for large-bore vascular access in patients with hostile or diminutive peripheral arteries [1]. While transfemoral access remains the default route for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), up to 15% of candidates have iliofemoral anatomy unsuitable for large sheaths owing to calcification, tortuosity, or small caliber [2]. Alternative access strategies—including transapical, transaxillary, transcarotid, and direct aortic—each carry distinct risks [3]. Transcaval access, in which the delivery system traverses from the inferior vena cava (IVC) into the abdominal aorta, has emerged as a percutaneous, fully endovascular alternative that avoids surgical incisions and thoracic violation [4].

## Concept and Rationale

Transcaval access exploits the close anatomic apposition of the IVC and the infrarenal abdominal aorta [5]. An electrified guidewire is advanced from the IVC across the aortic wall under fluoroscopic and venous-arterial co-registration, creating a controlled aorto-caval tract through which a large-bore sheath is delivered [6]. The pioneering preclinical and first-in-human work by Lederman and colleagues at the National Institutes of Health established the feasibility of crossing the aortic wall with electrosurgery and subsequently closing the tract with a nitinol occluder [7,8]. The physiological tolerance of an iatrogenic aorto-caval fistula—owing to the lower pressure gradient absorbed by the retroperitoneum and the self-limiting nature of bleeding into the venous system—underpins the safety of the technique [9].

## Procedural Technique

Preprocedural computed tomography is essential to identify a calcium-free target on the aortic wall and a suitable crossing trajectory, typically below the renal arteries and above the aortic bifurcation [10]. A snare or marker catheter is positioned in the aorta to serve as a fluoroscopic target, while a guidewire connected to an electrosurgical generator is advanced from a caval catheter [11]. After crossing, the wire is snared and externalized to establish a rail for sheath delivery [12]. Following completion of the structural intervention, the tract is closed using a nitinol duct occluder, with residual flow often sealing spontaneously [13]. Refinements in crossing catheters, dedicated closure devices, and imaging guidance have progressively simplified the workflow [14].

## Clinical Evidence

The prospective Transcaval Access Study demonstrated successful access in 99% and device closure in 96% of 100 patients undergoing TAVR with prohibitive alternative access [15]. Registry data have since confirmed reproducible outcomes across multiple centers [16,17]. Comparative analyses suggest transcaval access yields favorable mortality and morbidity relative to transapical and direct aortic approaches, in part by avoiding general anesthesia and thoracotomy [18,19]. A multicenter experience reported 30-day survival exceeding 90%, with most complications related to bleeding at the access tract rather than catastrophic aortic injury [20]. Beyond TAVR, transcaval access has facilitated delivery of mechanical circulatory support, thoracic endovascular aortic repair, and transcatheter mitral interventions requiring large sheaths [21,22].

## Complications and Management

The principal concern is retroperitoneal bleeding, which occurs in roughly 5–14% of cases and may require transfusion, covered-stent deployment, or rarely surgical repair [23]. Most bleeds arise from incomplete tract closure or lumbar artery injury and can be managed percutaneously [24]. Residual aorto-caval shunting after closure is usually small and clinically inconsequential, often resolving on follow-up imaging [25]. Appropriate patient selection guided by CT to avoid heavily calcified or aneurysmal aortic segments reduces complication rates [26]. Operator experience and adherence to standardized protocols are strong determinants of success [27].

## Future Directions

Dedicated transcaval closure devices, currently under investigation, promise to lower bleeding rates and broaden adoption [28]. Improved electrosurgical crossing systems and intracardiac or intravascular ultrasound guidance may further enhance precision [29]. As transcatheter therapies extend to younger and more complex patients, transcaval access is positioned to remain a valuable component of the structural heart operator's armamentarium, particularly where peripheral arterial access is precluded [30].

## Conclusion

Transcaval access has matured from an experimental concept into a clinically validated, percutaneous large-bore access strategy. With careful CT-based planning, reproducible crossing and closure techniques, and growing operator familiarity, it offers a compelling alternative for patients lacking transfemoral options. Ongoing device development is expected to consolidate its role across the breadth of structural heart interventions.
